artifact.source:
def f(x):
 a=[[1,2],[3,4]]
 b=a[:]
 a[0].append(x)
 a[1]=[5]
 return b

spec.explanation: a[:] creates a shallow copy: b gets a new outer list but shares the same inner lists. a[0].append(9) mutates the shared inner list, visible via b[0]. a[1]=[5] only rebinds a's slot, leaving b[1] as [3,4].

options.reason: The shallow copy shares inner lists, so append modifies b[0]. Rebinding a[1] does not affect b[1], which still holds [3,4].
This assumes rebinding a[1]=[5] also updates b[1], but the slice copy gives b its own reference to the original [3,4] object.
This assumes a[:] made a deep copy, but it only copies the outer list; inner lists remain shared, so append is visible through b[0].
This combines a deep-copy assumption for b[0] with a shared-reference assumption for b[1]—the opposite of what actually happens.

spec.topic: Shallow copy vs rebinding with nested lists

options.reason: The loop sums 2 and 3, then hits -1 and breaks. Break skips the for-else clause, so r remains 5.
